issues.legal_issue: The propounder of a will bears the burden of proving it and must remove legitimate suspicions surrounding its execution before the court accepts it as genuine.
material_facts: Executors sought probate of a will, and the testator’s relatives contested it on grounds including impaired mental capacity, undue influence, and allegedly inauthentic signatures.
The trial court found the testator’s and attesting witnesses’ signatures genuine, but refused probate because of doubts about the testator’s mental condition.
On appeal, the challenge to the genuineness of the signatures and the execution and attestation of the will was not pursued.
issues.conclusion: The propounder bears the onus of proving the will; proof of testamentary capacity and the testator’s signature, together with legally required attestation, ordinarily suffices where there are no suspicious circumstances. If suspicious circumstances arise, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction and satisfy the court’s conscience.
issues.legal_principle: The mode of proving a will ordinarily follows the mode of proving other documents, subject to the special attestation requirement in section 63 of the Succession Act. The propounder bears the onus, and suspicious circumstances—including concerns about signature, mental capacity, unnatural or unfair dispositions, or whether the testator’s mind was free—must be satisfactorily removed. A prominent role by a propounder who receives substantial benefit is also relevant. The Court followed Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, and Rani Purnima Devi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev.

predicates.probate_proceeding: A party seeks a court grant recognizing a purported will.
predicates.will_propounded: A party relies on a purported will as the basis for obtaining that grant.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances: Circumstances surrounding execution raise a legitimate doubt about the will’s authenticity, the testator’s capacity or freedom, or the fairness or naturalness of its dispositions.

issues.definition: When a party seeks recognition of a purported will and legitimate doubts surround its execution, the propounder must satisfactorily remove those doubts.

issues.legal_issue: The circumstances relied on in this case did not create unresolved suspicion about the will’s genuine execution or the testator’s capacity.
material_facts: The testator’s and attesting witnesses’ signatures were found genuine, and the will’s dispositions were found neither unfair nor unnatural.
The witnesses testified many years after execution, and the court considered their inability to recall particular dates understandable.

There was no evidence of an established practice requiring preservation of the draft or lawyer’s diary, and the relevant witnesses were not shown to have been withheld despite a demonstrated need to call them.
The use of known employees, a friend, and a relative as scribe or witnesses was considered normal; the medical evidence did not establish that the testator was comatose or had lost mental capacity.
A brother who received nothing under the will did not object to probate, the disposition was fair, and existing family litigation made a will intended to avoid future disputes plausible.
issues.conclusion: The alleged suspicious circumstances were either explained or were normal circumstances, and the evidence supported the will’s genuineness and valid execution; probate was properly granted.
issues.legal_principle: A circumstance is suspicious when it is abnormal, not normally expected in the situation, or not expected of a normal person. Suspicion does not require a court to persist in disbelief; the court must assess whether the circumstances are genuinely abnormal and whether any legitimate doubts have been removed. The Court applied the principles in Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, and Rani Purnima Devi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, and referred to Harmes v. Hinkson.

rule.if: probate_proceeding and testator_and_attesting_signatures_proved and no_evidence_of_lost_mental_capacity and disposition_fair_and_natural and alleged_irregularities_explained_or_normal and nonbeneficiary_relative_accepted_validity and family_dispute_made_will_plausible

predicates.probate_proceeding: A party seeks a court grant recognizing a purported will.
predicates.testator_and_attesting_signatures_proved: The evidence establishes the testator’s signature and the signatures of the witnesses who attested the will.
predicates.no_evidence_of_lost_mental_capacity: The evidence does not show that the testator lacked mental capacity when the will was executed.
predicates.disposition_fair_and_natural: The distribution in the will is fair and does not appear unnatural in the relevant circumstances.
predicates.alleged_irregularities_explained_or_norm: The claimed procedural or evidentiary irregularities are explained by the circumstances or reflect normal practice rather than abnormal conduct.
predicates.nonbeneficiary_relative_accepted_validit: A relative who received no benefit under the will accepted that it had been validly executed and attested.
predicates.family_dispute_made_will_plausible: Existing disputes among relatives made a will intended to prevent further disputes a plausible act.

issues.definition: Where the signatures and capacity are supported, the disposition is fair, the alleged irregularities are normal or explained, and other circumstances support the will, the will is accepted as genuine and probate is granted.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may review findings based on documentary inferences and may reverse a trial court’s refusal to grant probate when the evidence does not support the trial court’s suspicion.
material_facts: The trial court refused probate based on doubts about the testator’s mental condition despite finding the signatures genuine and the dispositions neither unfair nor unnatural.
The High Court reviewed the alleged suspicious circumstances, concluded that they were not suspicious or had been satisfactorily explained, and granted probate.
The Supreme Court found no suspicious circumstance surrounding execution and agreed that the trial court had been wrong to refuse probate.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in setting aside the trial court’s judgment and granting probate; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court should not lightly interfere where a trial judge’s conclusion depends on an impression formed from a witness’s testimony. But it may review an inferential process based on documents and circumstances, and should not uphold a factual conclusion unsupported by the evidence as a whole. The Court relied on The Bank of India Ltd. v. Jamsetji A.H. Chinoy and Madholal Sindhu v. Official Assignee of Bombay.

predicates.appeal_from_trial_judgment: A party appeals from a trial court’s judgment in a proceeding concerning a purported will.
predicates.trial_finding_based_on_inferences_from_d: The trial court’s finding rests on inferences drawn from documents and surrounding circumstances rather than solely on an impression of a witness.
predicates.evidence_as_a_whole_does_not_support_tri: The evidence considered as a whole does not substantiate the trial court’s conclusion that execution of the will was suspicious.

issues.definition: When a trial court’s suspicion rests on inferences from documents or circumstances and the evidence as a whole does not support it, an appellate court is justified in reversing that finding.
